Shipments that cross international borders are often subject to customs duties or tariffs, but sometimes they aren't. The product being shipped may be tax exempt. Or, the value of the shipment may be under the country of import's de minimis threshold.

What is a de minimis threshold?

Merriam-Webster defines "de minimis" as "lacking significance or importance." For cross-border commerce, a de minimis threshold is the minimum declared value a shipment must have for it to be subject to customs duty.

This isn't to say shipments valued at less than a country's duty de minimis threshold are insignificant. It simply means they're too small for that country to tax them upon entry: The tax that would be collected doesn't justify the cost of collecting it.

De minimis thresholds vary by country. Some countries have a generous (i.e., high) de minimis threshold, allowing more items to be imported tax free. In countries where the de minimis threshold is low, a greater number of imported goods are likely to be subject to customs duty and import taxes.

At $800, the de minimis threshold in the United States is high. Unless otherwise exempt, a shipment valued at $800 or more would be subject to U.S. customs duty upon entering the country, but no customs duty or import tax would be assessed on shipments valued at $799.99 or less.

Australia's de minimis threshold is also relatively high, at AUD 1,000 (about USD 679). By contrast, Canada's de minimis threshold of CAD 20 (about USD 14-15) is quite low. But it's not the lowest. There's no de minimis threshold in some countries, including Brazil and Iceland. Therefore, all shipments entering those countries are subject to customs duty unless otherwise exempt.

Because de minimis thresholds differ, shipments with the same value may be subject to duty in some countries but not in others. This adds to the complexity of cross-border selling.

De minimis thresholds for transaction taxes

In addition to having a de minimis threshold for customs duty, many countries have a de minimis threshold for value-added tax (VAT) or goods and services tax (GST). It may be the same as the de minimis threshold for customs duty, or it may be different.

For example, the de minimis threshold for customs duty is EUR 150 in France (about USD 167), but it's EUR 22 (about USD 25) for VAT. A cross-border shipment valued at EUR 100 would be exempt from France's duty and import taxes, but it would be subject to France's VAT, unless otherwise exempt.

As there's no nationwide sales tax in the U.S., there's no nationwide de minimis threshold for sales tax. However, shipments of taxable products are generally subject to applicable state and local sales taxes. If a retailer doesn't collect sales tax at checkout, the consumer must pay consumer use tax directly to state and/or local tax authorities.

How often do de minimis thresholds change?

De minimis thresholds in all countries can and do change, often as a result of geopolitical forces.

The definition of landed cost, also called landed price, is the total cost of getting a product from the supplier to its destination. Why Is Landed Cost Analysis Important?

It's crucial to conduct a landed cost analysis for all your shipments. It gives you a full picture of your costs and helps you make better-informed decisions. Calculating the landed cost is important because it provides you with a template on how to price your products.

Provides You More Accurate Information

What Are The Components of Landed Cost?

Several components account for the total cost in your ecommerce business. Product Cost

This is the cost of manufacturing or acquiring the product from manufacturers or suppliers. It accounts for the raw materials and other manufacturing components. You can reduce the product cost by streamlining your manufacturing processes, sourcing cheap raw material or obtaining supplies from manufacturers who sell the product at a favorable price, widening your profit margin.

Shipping

This includes the cost of transporting goods from suppliers to your fulfillment centers and then mailing packages to your customers. Handling fees, freight and transportation costs all make your shipping expenses. Depending on how you import and export your products, you may end up with varying shipping fees for inland, air or ocean freight. You can reduce shipping costs by negotiating better carrier rates, or partnering with 3PL (third-party logistics) providers that has multiple facilities so that your inventory is stored closer to your end customers. Although hidden fees can happen in domestic shipping, the term has come to be associated mostly with international shipping because of customs duties. Risk coverage is the fourth component. It has everything to do with protecting your cargo while it's in transit. The core mechanism you're being pitched is Section 321: any single shipment valued at $800 or less, addressed to one US recipient in one day, can enter duty-free and largely without formal customs clearance, which is exactly how Temu and Shein price so aggressively. [shard_04647_72515] [shard_00281_7313] Suppliers often package this as "ship from China to Mexico in bulk, hold it in a bonded warehouse just south of the border, then parcel it out under $800 per order," which keeps goods technically un-imported until the final cross-border hop to the customer. [shard_04647_72515] A similar version exists using a Canadian fulfillment company that receives bulk shipments from China, warehouses them, then ships single orders under $800 into the US to dodge the standard 25%-range tariff. [shard_01754_13790] The upside is real: eliminating duties, cutting formal entry paperwork, and speeding clearance can materially lower landed cost, and price is the main lever low-margin, low-differentiation categories like generic accessories compete on. [shard_04647_72515] [shard_05595_50615] But the fairness math cuts against you politically, since China's own de minimis threshold for inbound goods is roughly $7, versus $800 in the US, a gap lawmakers like Rep. Blumenauer have cited to justify tightening Section 321. [shard_01256_1845] Congress has multiple active bills aimed squarely at this loophole, including the Import Security and Fairness Act and the De Minimis Reciprocity Act, which would strip non-market economies like China of de minimis eligibility, restrict which carriers can file these entries, and require far more shipment data. [shard_03415_76201] Volume is also part of the problem: de minimis shipments have grown to roughly a billion-plus packages a year, and much of that flow rides on USPS's historically underpriced terminal-dues agreement with China Post, a subsidy dispute that led the US to withdraw from the Universal Postal Union in 2018 after posting an $80 million international-mail deficit. [shard_04965_57995] [shard_00641_34862] That subsidized-postage advantage is exactly what regulatory reform targets, so building your pricing model around it is building on ground that could shift under you with little notice. [shard_04965_57995] Not everyone agrees closing the loophole would rescue domestic manufacturing, though; one US textile-industry CEO argues the loophole actually squeezes big-box retailers like Walmart and Amazon far more than small manufacturers, and that 40 years of prior atrophy, not de minimis, explains most factory closures, a useful counterweight if you're worried this is an existential threat to small brands specifically. [shard_00294_59555] On delivery mechanics, air freight is the backbone of direct-to-consumer China shipping, and typical transit times run about 1-2 weeks for regular post, 3 days for air express, 8-10 days for standard air freight, and 30-40 days if anything slips to ocean, so your promised delivery windows are only as reliable as air cargo capacity. [shard_00864_19708] That capacity is genuinely strained: Temu alone was forecast to need roughly 2 million tonnes of cross-border air cargo, equivalent to about 40 Boeing 747s a day, which has already pushed freight rates up and given airlines more pricing leverage. [shard_03043_30847] E-commerce parcels also lean heavily on belly-cargo space in passenger jets, so unrelated shocks like the 737 MAX grounding can suddenly squeeze the exact aircraft type that carries small parcels. [shard_00769_76015] On compliance, the forced-labor risk is the sharpest edge here: the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act has no de minimis exception whatsoever, meaning even a $30 accessory can be detained if any part of its supply chain touches Xinjiang, and you'd bear the burden of "clear and convincing evidence" within 30 days to get it released. [shard_04073_1206] CBP itself has flagged that the sheer volume of low-value e-commerce parcels creates inspection gaps that criminal networks exploit specifically because interdiction risk is perceived as low, and counterfeit or unsafe goods do slip through, as in a real seizure of 1,900 boxes of Chinese holiday lights bearing fake UL safety marks. [shard_02403_59171] [shard_03938_37714] Given all that, the alternatives are worth taking seriously rather than treating China-direct as the default. Holding inventory in the US through a 3PL lets you use a multi-warehouse strategy that lowers shipping-zone costs and transit times, and reputable 3PLs increasingly offer networks spanning the US, Canada, Europe, and Asia so you're not locked into one country's rules. [shard_06311_34234] [shard_02377_73047] The honest way to compare options is landed cost, not just unit price: product cost, freight, customs, risk/insurance, and overhead all stack together, and a 3PL network can shrink the customs and shipping components simultaneously by fulfilling orders from the country closest to the buyer. [shard_04658_23662] Mexico and Canada nearshoring both still lean on the same $800 US threshold rather than a reciprocal foreign exemption, since Canada's own postal de minimis is only about CAD$20, rising to CAD$150 for courier shipments from the US or Mexico under CUSMA, so the "advantage" is really just relocating the Section-321 play one border closer, not escaping the underlying US policy risk. [shard_05049_78317] [shard_04577_14416] Cross-border trade between the US, Canada, and Mexico is enormous and growing, but shippers still report real friction from limited shipment visibility, seasonal truck-capacity shortages, and carrier-vetting requirements that a small brand would need a specialized partner to navigate. [shard_02971_35528] For a small accessories brand, the more durable path is treating China-direct de minimis shipping as a temporary arbitrage rather than a supply-chain foundation, using it selectively for testing or overflow while building US or near-US inventory positions, documented supplier sourcing away from Xinjiang-linked entities, and a brand identity strong enough that customers aren't just chasing the lowest possible per-unit price.
